pronunciation.approximation: Say "lada" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Lada".

kin.label: Slavic root *ladъ
kin.form: 'Order, harmony, concord' — the root scholars hear in her name; also a term of endearment in love-songs. Słownik prasłowiański; Afanasyev, Poetic Views of the Slavs on Nature (1865–1869).

kin.label: Lel and Polel
kin.form: The twin companions named beside her in the Kraków play Pogrzeb świętej Roksany and in Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582) — love flanked by play and youth.

kin.label: The folk cry 'lado'
kin.form: Refrain of South-Slavic Jurjevo / Đurđevdan spring round-dances, recorded by nineteenth-century ethnographers; the feminine Lada may be its personification.

pronunciation.note: Lada is Tier 2: the ASCII form 'lada' is already the full Latin spelling, and the restoration adds nothing distinctive that DNS would lose. What the record lacks is not diacritics but early attestations — every source naming Lada postdates Christianization by centuries.

domains.title: Lada
domains.subtitle: Love
domains.lead: Lada is the Slavic goddess of love, harmony, and spring — or perhaps a folk-song cry that the chroniclers turned into a goddess. Every written source naming her is late: medieval glosses, a Renaissance school play, and spring refrains sung on Jurjevo (St George's Day). Her divine status is debated; her presence in the song tradition is not.

cards.name: Sacred Name
cards.desc: The name rides on Slavic *ladъ, 'order, harmony, concord' — love conceived as the harmonizing force, not mere desire.

cards.name: Love
cards.desc: Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582) names her the Slavic goddess of love; folk tradition keeps her in wedding songs as the beloved 'lado'.

cards.name: Living Tradition
cards.desc: Her oldest witnesses are alive: the refrain 'Lado!' still rings through Đurđevdan / Jurjevo round-dances in the Balkans each May.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

symbols.name: The spring round dance (kolo)
symbols.meaning: Lado is sung inside the circle dance that opens the grazing season on Jurjevo — the goddess lives in the choreography, not the statue.

symbols.name: Jurjevo / Đurđevdan (St George's Day)
symbols.meaning: The spring feast whose songs carry her name, absorbed into folk Christianity as St George's day, 6 May.

symbols.name: Lel and Polel
symbols.meaning: The twin companions named beside her in the Roksana play and the chronicles — love flanked by play and youth.

symbols.name: Green branches (zelenika)
symbols.meaning: The green oak bough ritually cut for Jurjevo and carried to the pasture — the spring rite's portable sacred tree.

symbols.name: *ladъ — harmony
symbols.meaning: Her name's root: concord, good order, the reconciliation of lovers — love as cosmic harmony made audible.

mythology.lead: No medieval Slavic text tells a myth of Lada. What survives is a trail of witnesses — a funeral play, a chronicler's glosses, Renaissance mythography, and living spring songs — from which scholarship must carefully separate memory from invention. Her 'mythology' is therefore the history of how a song-cry became a goddess, and an honest temple must tell it that way.

myths.title: The Refrain in the Round Dance
myths.text:
The oldest trace of Lada is not a story about her but a word sung in her place. In the spring round-dances of the South Slavs on Jurjevo — St George's Day, 6 May, when the grazing season opens — the cry Lado! punctuates the melody: greeting, praise, chorus, or the goddess herself, the sources never say. Young people cut the green oak, the zelenika, dance around it, and carry it to the pasture; nineteenth-century ethnographers among Croats, Serbs, and the Balkan Roma recorded the songs with the refrain intact. Farther north the same word softens into endearment: in Polish and Ukrainian wedding songs ladko and lado mean simply 'dear one.' The earliest stratum of the evidence is thus not narrative but music.

If Lada was ever a full goddess, her first body was a song — which is why she has survived every empire that buried her chroniclers.

myths.title: Lada, Lel, and Polel on the Stage
myths.text:
The first text to list Lada among the gods is a joke at her expense. The Kraków school drama Pogrzeb świętej Roksany ('The Funeral of St. Roxane'), composed around 1500 and printed in 1535, brings together three students — a German, a Czech, and a Pole — to argue over whose hero deserves burial. The Pole defends his own ancestors: our gods, he insists, were Lada, Lel, and Polel, and our songs still remember them. The comedy mocks him for clinging to heathenry; but mockery preserves what reverence forgot, and the schoolboy's boast is now our earliest catalogue of Slavic divine names. The sources disagree even here: the play pairs Lada with Lel and Polel, while later writers split the twins differently and added genealogies no one attests.

A goddess remembered in ridicule is still remembered — the play is less evidence of cult than of a name refusing, two centuries after conversion, to disappear.

myths.title: The Glosses of Długosz and His Successors
myths.text:
Jan Długosz, the fifteenth-century Polish annalist, inserted into his Annales (Book I) marginal glosses on the old religion: the pagan Poles, he claims, used Lado for God himself, and among their goddesses he names Lada — glossing her, erratically, as Venus. The glosses, transmitted in the copy made by Stanisław Komasius, equate the native names so inconsistently that no modern scholar trusts the identifications. Later Renaissance mythography repeated and inflated them: Marcin Kromer's Polonia (1555), Maciej Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582) — which makes Lada a goddess of love — and Stanisław Sarnicki (1585) and Szymon Starowolski (1615), who repeat the lore with growing confidence. None of them cites a source older than folk memory.

The chroniclers did not record Lada; they manufactured her — a caution this temple must carry at its threshold.

myths.title: Goddess or Refrain?
myths.text:
The nineteenth century decided the question by enthusiasm. Alexander Afanasyev's Poetic Views of the Slavs on Nature (1865–1869) enthroned Lada as a great goddess of spring and love, flanked by her twin sons Lel and Polel; Šafařík and Krek spread the picture across Slavdom, and Romantic art gave her a face. Twentieth-century scholarship pulled back hard: Michał Gieysztor's Mitologia Słowian (1982) keeps her cautiously, while Leszek P. Słupecki's Religia Słowian (2018) and other critics argue that the attestations are too late and too folkloric — that lado may never have been more than a refrain-word, with Lada its feminine form, like the wedding cry ladno still heard in Serbia. Comparatists set her beside the Greek Horai and the Latvian Laima, but no genetic link can be proven.

The tradition is fragmentary and the sources openly disagree — and the debate itself, still alive, is the closest thing Lada has ever had to a cult.

lore.syncretism: Later ages never found a Roman Lada to match her to, so they invented one: Długosz and Stryjkowski gloss her as Venus, Kromer as a love-goddess, and the equation stuck — every early-modern portrait of Lada is Venus in Slavic dress. The honest parallels are structural: the Greek Horai, guardians of spring's order, and the Latvian Laima, who apportions luck and love, fill her functional niche in neighbouring traditions, though no borrowing can be shown. Folk Christianity absorbed her feast without noticing her: Jurjevo became Đurđevdan, St George's Day, and the Balkan Roma keep the same spring festival as Ederlezi. The twentieth century added a final layer: Rodnovery, the modern Slavic Native Faith, enthrones Lada as a supreme goddess of love and cosmic harmony — a reconstruction built, openly and defiantly, on the refrains and the chroniclers alike.
lore.culturalLegacy: Lada's cult centers are songs, not ruins: Jurjevo and Đurđevdan round-dances in Croatia, Serbia, and Bosnia; the Roma Ederlezi, when spring is ritually opened with the green oak; Kupala's fires on St John's Eve in Poland, Belarus, and Ukraine — a sister spring festival whose own antiquity is equally debated. Her name fared better in the dictionary than in the temple: Polish ład 'order, tidiness', Czech lad 'harmony, proportion', and the adjective ladný 'graceful' all descend from the same *ladъ that scholars hear in her name — love as concord made audible. Romanticism painted her on salon canvases; Slavic Native Faith circles hail her today at wedding rites and spring gatherings. No inscription marks her grave because none marks her birth: Lada lives wherever Slavic speakers still sing lado over a bride or a green branch.
lore.extendedMeditation: Most goddesses in this lexicon were carved, inscribed, or sung into epics; Lada survives in the one medium memory never loses — the chorus. Hers is a strange immortality: the sources that name her are late, contradictory, and partly fraudulent, yet the refrain they record is older than any of them, still sung on a Balkan hillside every May. The lesson she teaches is about evidence itself. A word repeated at weddings and spring fires for a thousand years need not have been a god to be holy; ritual can consecrate a syllable. To study Lada is to watch scholarship and devotion negotiate: the scholar asks 'goddess or refrain?', the grandmother answers 'Lado!' — and both are keeping the tradition alive, which may be what tradition is. Her temple, honestly built, is a round dance with no image at its center.
lore.archaeology: No material object can be assigned to Lada, and the catalogue says so plainly: no pre-Christian inscription, figurine, or cult site names her, and the so-called Slavic idols — the Zbruch figure and its kin — depict no identifiable goddess of love. Her 'archaeology' is the archaeology of performance: green-oak branches (zelenika) ritually cut and carried to pasture on Jurjevo, round-dance grounds, and the ritual calendar of Đurđevdan. The written witnesses are manuscripts, not monuments: Długosz's Annales in the Komasius copy (16th century), the 1535 print of Pogrzeb świętej Roksany, and Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582). A goddess whose entire dossier is paper, wax, and song must be honored differently from one with temples — her material record is a living spring.
